To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
enzymes can control the activity of other proteins in a substrate‐dependent manner and that this is a widespread mechanism to regulate gene expression in bacteria.
enzymes can control transcription and translation by sensing the availability of their metabolites.
enzymes can act as sensors and control gene expression in bacteria by four different mechanisms.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the mechanisms by which enzymes are recruited for the regulation of gene expression.
the molecular mechanisms of gene regulation.
the evolution of the regulatory mechanisms in bacteria, and we are interested in the molecular basis of these regulatory mechanisms.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

enzymes can control the expression of other genes in the absence of any other regulatory protein, and that this control is mediated by a specific interaction with a DNA‐binding protein, a small regulatory RNA, a protein kinase or a protein‐protein interaction.
enzymes are not just enzymes, but can be active in the regulation of their own synthesis.
enzymes can control the expression of other genes in response to their metabolic state.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the trigger enzyme concept is an important new concept in the study of the control of gene regulation in bacteria.
enzymes can be involved in the control of their own expression as well as in the regulation of other genes.
the trigger enzymes have evolved to sense the environmental conditions of the cell and to control gene expression accordingly.
The main takeaway from our work is that
trigger enzymes are a major class of regulatory proteins that have evolved in all domains of life.
the control of gene regulation by trigger enzymes may be a common mechanism in bacteria and that this mechanism may also be present in eukaryotes, although the evidence for this is less convincing.
trigger enzymes have evolved as an additional layer of regulation that allows the cell to control the fluxes of metabolites in response to environmental changes.
